exact_claim: Assignment to Mediterranean diet + EVOO or nuts associated with lower major CV events vs reduced-fat advice in high-risk adults without baseline CVD
diet_definition: Mediterranean diet (energy-unrestricted) supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil (~1 L/week free provision) or mixed nuts (~30 g/day free provision); quarterly education. Control: advice to reduce dietary fat with small nonfood gifts.
population_definition: Spanish adults 55-80 years, high CV risk (type 2 diabetes or ≥3 risk factors), free of CVD at enrollment; 57% women; multicenter.
study_type: Multicenter trial with protocol deviations in randomization; reanalyzed as non-exclusively randomized with propensity-score adjustment (intention-to-treat including all).
comparison: Med + EVOO or Med + nuts vs control reduced-fat advice
followup: Median 4.8 years (stopped early on interim analysis)
outcome: Composite major CV event (MI, stroke, or CV death)
effect_size_and_CI: Med+EVOO: 96/2543 events (3.8%), HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.91); Med+nuts: 83/2454 (3.4%), HR 0.72 (0.54-0.95); control: 109/2450 (4.4%). Similar after excluding 1588 with known/suspected deviations.
p_value_if_relevant: Not primary focus of revised report; original 2013 stopped early.
errata_status: 2013 original retracted (NEJM 2018;378:2441-2); 2018 republication with revised analyses not assuming full randomization. Protocol deviations: household members enrolled without randomization, some site assignment issues, inconsistent randomization tables.
risk_of_bias: High (randomization problems, early stopping, control diet intensity lower).
quality_of_evidence: Moderate for composite CV events after reanalysis (hard endpoint, large n); lower for subgroups.
limits_and_harms: Early stopping; control was not an intensive low-fat diet; Spanish high-risk population; free food provision may aid adherence; no clear total mortality benefit in revised analyses (see figure data: EVOO HR 0.90 [0.69-1.18], nuts 1.12 [0.86-1.47]).
transportability: Limited to Spanish primary-prevention high-risk adults; cultural food availability and education intensity matter.
app_safe_statement: In one large Spanish trial of high-risk adults free of CVD, Mediterranean patterns with free olive oil or nuts showed lower rates of major heart events than reduced-fat advice after accounting for randomization issues; results do not prove the pattern replaces medication or applies identically elsewhere.
no_personal_inference: No inference that any individual will experience the same absolute risk reduction.
cross_team_dependencies: None for this claim; secondary publications exist but primary endpoint revised.

exact_claim: Mediterranean diet superior to low-fat diet for major CV events in secondary prevention.
diet_definition: Mediterranean diet vs low-fat diet; dietitian-delivered intensive counseling; both energy-unrestricted.
population_definition: Spanish patients with established coronary heart disease, age 20-75 (mean 59.5), 82.5% men; single center (Córdoba).
study_type: Randomized controlled trial (1:1, masked endpoint assessment).
outcome: Composite major CV events (MI, revascularization, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, CV death)
effect_size_and_CI: 87/502 Med vs 111/500 low-fat; crude rates 28.1 vs 37.7 per 1000 person-years; multivariable-adjusted HRs 0.719 (0.541-0.957) to 0.753 (0.568-0.998). More evident in men (HR 0.669 [0.489-0.915]).
risk_of_bias: Low-moderate (single-center, open to participants, high male proportion).
quality_of_evidence: Moderate-high for secondary-prevention composite (hard events, longer follow-up).
limits_and_harms: Single center Spain; predominantly male; adherence not universal; women underpowered (no difference observed).
transportability: Spanish secondary-prevention population; transportability to other ethnicities or lower-intensity counseling uncertain.
app_safe_statement: In patients with existing coronary disease, a Mediterranean pattern was linked to fewer major cardiovascular events than a low-fat pattern over 7 years in one Spanish trial; this supports discussion with clinicians, not automatic replacement of therapy.
no_personal_inference: No personal risk prediction or claim that diet replaces drugs.

exact_claim: DASH diet + lower sodium lowers systolic BP more than either alone, especially in hypertensives.
diet_definition: DASH diet (vegetables, fruits, low-fat dairy, reduced saturated fat/cholesterol) vs control typical US diet; crossed with high/intermediate/low sodium (30 days each, random order).
population_definition: US adults with and without hypertension (412 total); mixed race/sex.
comparison: DASH vs control diet × sodium levels
effect_size_and_CI: DASH + low Na vs control + high Na: SBP −11.5 mm Hg (hypertensives), −7.1 mm Hg (normotensives). Sodium reduction effects additive but smaller on DASH background.
p_value_if_relevant: Multiple p<0.05 for sodium steps and DASH differences.
quality_of_evidence: High for short-term BP (surrogate); not hard events.
limits_and_harms: Short-term only; free food; long-term adherence and hard outcomes not tested here; effects larger in some subgroups (e.g., Black participants noted in related work).
transportability: US adults; feeding conditions not identical to free-living.
app_safe_statement: Controlled feeding showed the DASH pattern plus lower sodium reduced blood pressure more than either change alone in adults with and without high blood pressure; blood pressure is a risk marker, not a heart-event count.
no_personal_inference: No claim of individualized BP drop or that diet replaces antihypertensive drugs.

exact_claim: Portfolio pattern + NCEP Step II reduces LDL-C ~17% and other lipids/BP/CRP vs Step II alone.
diet_definition: Portfolio: plant sterols, soy protein, viscous fiber, nuts on background of NCEP Step II (low saturated fat).
population_definition: Hyperlipidemic adults; 7 trial comparisons, total 439 participants.
study_type: Systematic review + meta-analysis of controlled trials (≥3 weeks).
comparison: Portfolio + Step II vs Step II alone (energy-matched)
outcome: LDL-C (primary surrogate); also non-HDL-C, ApoB, TG, SBP/DBP, CRP, estimated 10-yr CHD risk
effect_size_and_CI: LDL-C MD −0.73 mmol/L (95% CI −0.89 to −0.56); ~17% reduction. Significant reductions in listed markers (p<0.05); no effect on HDL-C or weight.
risk_of_bias: Low-moderate (included trials mostly short, some metabolic ward).
quality_of_evidence: High for LDL-C and most lipids (GRADE); moderate for BP/CRP/estimated risk.
limits_and_harms: Surrogate endpoints only; no hard CV events in the meta-analysis; adherence determines magnitude; short duration relative to disease processes.
transportability: Hyperlipidemic adults in controlled settings; free-living adherence lower.
app_safe_statement: Combining plant sterols, soy, viscous fiber, and nuts with a low-saturated-fat background lowered LDL cholesterol more than the low-saturated-fat diet alone in short controlled trials; this is a cholesterol marker change, not a count of heart attacks.
no_personal_inference: No claim that Portfolio replaces statin therapy or produces the same drop in every person.

exact_claim: No significant difference in 12-month weight loss between healthy low-fat and healthy low-carb; no genotype or insulin interaction.
diet_definition: Healthy low-fat (emphasize vegetables, lean proteins, whole grains; fat ~29% at 12 mo) vs healthy low-carb (emphasize vegetables, proteins, fats; carb ~30% at 12 mo); both quality-focused, not extreme.
population_definition: US adults 18-50 years, BMI 28-40, no diabetes; 57% women; mean age ~40.
effect_size_and_CI: −5.3 kg (low-fat) vs −6.0 kg (low-carb); between-group difference 0.7 kg (95% CI −0.2 to 1.6). No diet-genotype (P=0.20) or diet-INS-30 (P=0.47) interaction.
risk_of_bias: Low-moderate (self-selected free-living, ~20% calorie reduction both arms).
quality_of_evidence: High for null between-diet weight difference and null interactions in this population.
limits_and_harms: Weight is surrogate; large individual variability (−30 to +10 kg range reported); quality focus may differ from ultra-processed low-fat or extreme low-carb.
app_safe_statement: In one year-long trial of overweight adults without diabetes, average weight loss was similar on a quality-focused low-fat pattern and a quality-focused low-carbohydrate pattern; neither genotype pattern nor baseline insulin secretion predicted which diet produced more loss.
no_personal_inference: No claim that any person is genetically suited to one macronutrient pattern or that weight change is guaranteed.

exact_claim: DASH, Mediterranean, pescetarian, and ovo-lacto vegetarian patterns show strongest alignment with 2021 AHA heart-healthy guidance.
diet_definition: DASH-style, Mediterranean-style, pescetarian, ovo-lacto vegetarian, vegan, low-fat, very-low-fat, low-carb, paleo, very-low-carb/keto.
population_definition: US popular dietary patterns evaluated against AHA 2021 criteria (not a trial population).
study_type: Scientific statement / expert alignment scoring (not new primary data).
comparison: Alignment scores vs AHA guidance features
outcome: Alignment with heart-healthy pattern features (guidance concordance)
effect_size_and_CI: DASH 100; pescetarian 92; Mediterranean 89; ovo-lacto vegetarian 86; vegan and low-fat 78 each. Paleo and keto lowest.
quality_of_evidence: Moderate as expert synthesis of existing evidence + practical factors.
limits_and_harms: Alignment ≠ proven hard-event reduction; cultural/budget factors noted as important for adherence; vegan notes B12 risk.
transportability: US context; adaptable to cultural preferences per statement.
app_safe_statement: A 2023 AHA statement rated DASH, Mediterranean, pescetarian, and vegetarian patterns as closely matching its 2021 heart-healthy guidance; ratings reflect guidance alignment, not new trial results on heart attacks.
no_personal_inference: No claim that alignment score predicts individual event rates.
cross_team_dependencies: Depends on underlying trials (PREDIMED, DASH, etc.).

exact_claim: Vegetarian vs non-vegetarian associated with lower CVD and IHD in prospective cohorts.
diet_definition: Vegetarian (various definitions, often lacto-ovo) vs non-vegetarian.
study_type: Systematic review + meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
quality_of_evidence: Low-moderate (cohorts; no primary RCTs for hard events on pure vegetarian).
limits_and_harms: Observational; cannot prove causation; residual confounding by lifestyle; definitions of vegetarian vary; stroke null.
transportability: Mixed populations; transportability depends on overall lifestyle.
app_safe_statement: In observational cohorts, people following vegetarian patterns had lower rates of heart disease diagnoses than non-vegetarians; this is association, not proof that switching diet causes the difference.
no_personal_inference: No inference of causality or individual outcome.

exact_claim: Low-fat pattern (target 20% energy from fat + more veg/fruit/grains) did not significantly reduce overall CHD/stroke/CVD vs usual diet in postmenopausal women.
diet_definition: Low-fat dietary pattern intervention (fat reduction + increased vegetables, fruit, grains) vs usual diet.
population_definition: Postmenopausal US women 50-79 years, baseline fat ≥32% energy; 48835 total.
followup: Mean ~8.1 years intervention; longer follow-up available
effect_size_and_CI: Intervention vs comparison: CHD HR 0.97 (0.90-1.06); stroke 1.02 (0.90-1.15); CVD 0.98 (0.92-1.05). Subgroup: normotensive no prior CVD showed lower CHD in some analyses.
risk_of_bias: Low-moderate (large pragmatic, modest fat reduction achieved).
quality_of_evidence: Moderate for null overall hard events in this population.
limits_and_harms: Achieved fat difference ~8-10% energy; control was usual diet not intensive; some subgroup signals (and possible confounding by post-randomization meds); stroke signal in some analyses.
app_safe_statement: In a large trial of postmenopausal women, advice to lower fat and raise vegetables, fruit, and grains did not significantly change overall heart-attack or stroke rates compared with usual diet over about 8 years.
no_personal_inference: No claim that low-fat is harmful or protective for every woman.
